summary: A 1977 Telnet option for data entry terminals. It was replaced by RFC 732.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 731 defines a Telnet option for data-entry terminals with rectangular screens and form fields. The option lets the two sides negotiate supported features and exchange screen-control commands separately from ordinary text.

subtitle: A Telnet option for controlling data-entry terminals over a network connection.

tldr.problem: Data-entry terminals use screen fields and cursor controls that ordinary Telnet text transmission does not describe.
tldr.mechanism: The DET Telnet option defines subcommands for negotiating terminal facilities, moving the cursor, formatting and erasing fields, and transmitting screen data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 731 is an early Telnet option specification and was obsoleted by RFC 732.

sections.title: The Data-Entry Terminal Option
sections.content:
The Telnet option is named DET and has option code 20. It describes a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal with a keyboard and a rectangular display. Fields may have attributes such as blinking, reverse video, intensity, or protection from user modification.

The option uses Telnet subnegotiations for control functions rather than reserving ASCII data characters for those functions. Peripheral devices such as printers are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: DET gives Telnet a way to control form-style terminals, including their cursor and protected fields. Control commands use Telnet subnegotiation rather than ordinary text characters.

sections.title: Negotiating Terminal Facilities
sections.content:
The option defines facility subcommands for editing, erasing, transmission, and formatting. A facility map describes features a terminal provides or an application requests, such as cursor movement, line insertion and deletion, blinking, and field protection.

An implementation must negotiate facilities outside the minimal set before using them. The parties use the intersection of requested and provided facilities to determine which features are available.
sections.plainLanguage: The terminal and application first agree on which optional features they both support. An application must not use a non-minimal feature before negotiating it.

sections.title: Screen Editing and Data Transmission
sections.content:
The subcommands include absolute cursor movement, line and character insertion or deletion, screen and field erasure, and formatting data with attributes. Cursor movement can use a finite plane or toroidal screen topology, depending on negotiated facilities.

Transmission commands can send the whole screen, a line, a field, or unprotected fields. The RFC's minimal implementation includes facility negotiation, moving and homing the cursor, erasing the screen, transmitting the screen, formatting data, and reporting errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands can edit the screen and mark fields, then send all or selected screen data back. The RFC also specifies a small required set of functions for a minimal implementation.
